chunks.title: About Ali Rad
chunks.text: Ali Rad is a Computer Engineering student at Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, graduating in December 2028. He researches TMS neuronavigation in the Khavari Lab at Houston Methodist and viral genome annotation in the Neuman Lab, and builds embedded systems, computer vision, and full-stack software. He works in C++, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Java and SQL. He is seeking summer 2027 internships.

chunks.title: AliBot
chunks.text: AliBot is a project by Ali Rad. Status: Live. A RAG chatbot for this site, running as a TypeScript Cloudflare Worker. It combines vector search with BM25, reranks the results with a cross-encoder, and has Llama 3.3 70B answer only from the retrieved sources, with citations. A 33-question eval set measures retrieval recall, citation accuracy, and prompt-injection resistance: 100% recall@4 at 1.9 s median latency. Stack: TypeScript · Cloudflare Workers · Vectorize · Workers AI. Tags: Live, TypeScript, Cloudflare, RAG, Astro. Links: How it works: https://github.com/alirad1/alirad.dev/blob/master/alibot/README.md, Source: https://github.com/alirad1/alirad.dev/tree/master/alibot.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav
chunks.text: TMS-Nav (Khavari Lab) is a project by Ali Rad. Status: Live. Research software for comparing EEG 10–20 cap targeting with MRI-guided TMS neuronavigation. A Python pipeline builds scalp meshes from T1 MRI, places 10–20 electrode sites by arc length, and runs Monte Carlo sampling of coil placement error. Recorded Brainsight poses feed the placement statistics, a SimNIBS workflow models the induced electric field, and a Three.js viewer shows the results in 3D. Stack: Python · NiBabel · SimNIBS · Three.js. Tags: Live, Python, JavaScript, Three.js. Links: Open viewer: https://tms-nav.github.io/TMS-Nav/, Source: https://github.com/TMS-Nav/TMS-Nav.

chunks.text: Ali Rad — Researcher, TMS neuronavigation at Khavari Lab, May 2026 – Present, Houston Methodist, Houston, TX. This is part of Ali's research and work experience. Independent project under a Rice University PhD student comparing EEG 10–20 cap positioning with MRI-guided neuronavigation for figure-8 TMS coil placement in rTMS treatment of neurogenic overactive bladder. I quantify placement accuracy with Monte Carlo sampling and paired equivalence testing, and built a SimNIBS model of the electric field each method delivers to the cortical target from subject MRI. The question is whether the lower-cost cap method is clinically equivalent and could widen access to rTMS. Topics: TMS, Neuroimaging, SimNIBS, Statistics. More: https://tms-nav.github.io/TMS-Nav/.

chunks.title: AliBot — What it is
chunks.text: AliBot is a small chat assistant docked in the corner of this site. It answers questions about Ali's projects and experience using only the content on alirad.dev and the README of each project repository. Every answer carries citations, and clicking one scrolls to the exact card or entry the sentence came from. If the retrieved sources do not answer a question, AliBot says so instead of guessing. It was built to practise retrieval-augmented generation end to end rather than to wire up a chat box around a general-purpose model.

chunks.title: AliBot — How retrieval works
chunks.text: The corpus is generated from the same data file the site renders, so a chunk id always matches an element on the page. A question is embedded with bge-base-en-v1.5 into a 768-dimension vector and searched against Cloudflare Vectorize for the twelve nearest chunks. In parallel the Worker runs BM25 keyword scoring over the bundled corpus for its own top twelve. The two ranked lists are combined with reciprocal rank fusion, which rewards chunks that both methods rank highly without needing the two score scales to be comparable. The fused top eight then go through a cross-encoder reranker, bge-reranker-base, which reads the question and each chunk together and scores real relevance rather than vector proximity. The best four become the sources for the answer.

chunks.title: AliBot — How answers are generated
chunks.text: The four reranked chunks are numbered and placed in the system prompt, and the model is instructed to answer only from them and to mark each sentence with the number of the source it used. Generation runs on Llama 3.3 70B through Workers AI with streaming enabled, so tokens reach the browser over server-sent events as they are produced. The bracketed numbers in the finished answer are swapped for citation chips in the widget. Answers are capped at 400 tokens and run at a low temperature, because the job is to report what the sources say, not to write freely.

chunks.title: AliBot — Guardrails
chunks.text: A grounding gate sits between retrieval and generation: if the best reranker score falls below a threshold tuned against the eval set, AliBot declines without calling the model at all, which makes an off-topic question both safer and free. The question is capped at 500 characters and the history at six turns. Visitor text only ever appears in the user turn of the prompt, never spliced into the system instructions, and the sources are Ali’s own content rather than arbitrary web pages. Model output is rendered as text nodes, never as HTML, so nothing it produces can execute in the page. A rate-limit binding allows ten questions per minute per address.

chunks.title: AliBot — Evaluation
chunks.text: A thirty-question golden set runs against the deployed Worker: twenty questions that the site can answer, each labelled with the chunk that should be retrieved, six that it should refuse as out of scope, and four prompt-injection attempts. The harness records recall at four, the share of answers that cite a real source, how reliably out-of-scope questions are declined, resistance to injection, and the latency and neuron cost of every turn. Choosing between the 70B and 8B models was settled by running the same set against both rather than by preference.

chunks.title: AliBot — What it costs
chunks.text: Nothing, structurally. The Worker, the Vectorize index and the inference all sit on Cloudflare free tiers, and there is no payment method on the account, so exceeding the daily allowance of ten thousand neurons returns an error rather than a bill. When that happens AliBot falls back to returning the retrieved sections verbatim with their citations, which needs no model call. The widget still reports what each answer would have cost at the paid rate, because an assistant whose price you cannot see is an assistant you cannot reason about.

chunks.title: AliBot README: How it fits together
chunks.text: AliBot README — How it fits together. All of the content lives as data in src/data/site.ts. The page in src/pages/index.astro maps over those arrays and renders them through small components in src/components/, so adding a project or an experience entry is an edit to one file rather than a block of markup to copy out by hand. Styling is written by hand in src/styles/, and everything static (the images, the favicon, robots, sitemap) sits in public/. Keeping the content apart from the presentation like this is really the whole idea. The site reads as one measured page, and the parts that repeat are described once and reused.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: TMS-Nav
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — TMS-Nav. Compare EEG cap targeting with MRI-guided TMS neuronavigation. Build scalp meshes, place approximate study targets and coils, and explore Monte Carlo placement variability in a Three.js viewer. Recorded Brainsight poses support the Aim 1 geometric comparison; a separate SimNIBS workflow supports Aim 2 electric-field modeling. The MNI demo and simulated placements are for development and illustration. Template targets are anatomical approximations, not individualized fMRI targets. Individual subjects use a separate cached reconstruction pipeline with reviewable MRI fiducial candidates, native scalp meshes, manual landmark confirmation and subject-specific EEG estimates. See the complete subject workflow and verification report.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Quick start
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Quick start. Use Python 3.12 (the verified local version) and Node.js 22 LTS or newer with npm. Run these commands from the repository root after cloning it.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Preferred micromamba environment
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Preferred micromamba environment. Python 3.12 and Node 22 were verified in tms312. The environment file includes a Linux library for browser tests; omit alsa-lib on other platforms. The alternative venv instructions below remain available. MNI assets are generated once; subjects then require only native T1w, with no fMRI or registration prerequisite.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Windows PowerShell
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Windows PowerShell. powershell py -3.12 -m venv venv .\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip .\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt .\venv\Scripts\python.exe runpipeline.py cd viewer npm.cmd ci npm.cmd run dev

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: macOS and Linux
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — macOS and Linux. bash python3.12 -m venv venv ./venv/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade pip ./venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt ./venv/bin/python runpipeline.py cd viewer npm ci npm run dev Open the local viewer. These commands use the venv directly, so activation and PowerShell execution-policy changes are unnecessary. After activating a venv yourself, python can replace the interpreter paths below. Linux distributions may require their Python venv package. Headless rendering requires a working VTK graphics backend (EGL/OSMesa or an X display, depending on the VTK build); off-screen mode alone does not provide that backend.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: MRI inputs and template fallback
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — MRI inputs and template fallback. bash python runpipeline.py # saves/ scans, otherwise MNI152 python runpipeline.py --template # force the MNI152 demo python runpipeline.py saves/cohorts/ms # one cohort, searched recursively python runpipeline.py saves/cohorts/ms saves/cohorts/control python runpipeline.py "/path/to/subjectT1w.nii.gz" With no arguments, the pipeline searches saves/ for structural scans, including nested cohorts. If none are found, or the supplied folders contain no eligible scans, it downloads and uses the full-head ICBM152 2009a T1 template. The first template run needs internet access; later runs reuse saves/templates/. The fetcher downloads an approximately 63 MB archive with several template images; only the unmasked T1 is processed. The cache is excluded from patient discovery. A nonexistent path or unsupported explicit file produces an error. NiBabel loads NIfTI data and the affine but has no MNI downloader. Downloads use nilearn.datasets.fetchicbm1522009. The bundled loadmni152template is skull-stripped and does not supply the scalp needed here. For patient scans:

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: MRI inputs and template fallback
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — MRI inputs and template fallback. - Supply a T1-weighted structural NIfTI (.nii or .nii.gz) with scalp and external head anatomy. Convert DICOM to NIfTI beforehand. - Prefer intact facial anatomy and ears. Defaced scans are supported and flagged, but missing anatomy cannot be recovered and landmarks become approximate. - Preserve a valid spatial affine in millimeters. Landmark heuristics assume a head approximately aligned with anatomical RAS directions; all proposed landmarks require review. - Approximately 1 mm resolution is preferred; anisotropic spacing is supported and no exact voxel size is enforced. - Native subjects require 3D volumes, explicit spatial units and consistent coded qform/sform metadata. Ambiguous headers and 4D inputs are rejected. - Store only intended structural inputs in discovery folders. The pipeline does not identify contrast: T2, fMRI, mask and segmentation NIfTIs would also be selected.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Local data layout
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Local data layout. Legacy saves/.nii and saves/.nii.gz inputs remain supported. For multiple cohorts, use one structural scan per subject, or distinct filenames for visits: Discovery skips templates, previews, brainsight, aim1, efield, m2m, derivatives, m2m folders and hidden directories. Explicit paths are resolved from the current working directory. Default inputs and all outputs are anchored to the repository, so the script can also run from another directory.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Outputs and viewer compatibility
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Outputs and viewer compatibility. The MNI demo produces front/side PNGs and a distance histogram in saves/previews/. Subjects produce slice QC, reusable native derivatives and confidence reports in saves/derivatives/subjects//. The viewer retains its per-dataset structure: Legacy T1.nii.gz still maps to data/T1/. Cohort paths map to names such as mssub-001T1w and controlsub-001T1w, keeping shared subject IDs separate. Characters outside letters, digits, , - and . become underscores. Resulting name collisions are rejected before processing. Explicit inputs outside saves/ use their filenames as dataset names. viewer/src/datasetRegistry.js is regenerated from all existing processed dataset folders, giving Parcel static imports. Reruns overwrite matching outputs and keep other datasets. Removing or renaming an input does not delete old viewer output: remove its generated dataset folder, then rerun to update the dropdown. saves/ and viewer/src/data/ are Git-ignored. Patient scans and derived meshes stay local. Cohort discovery currently applies to runpipeline.py; the separate statistics and electric-field drivers retain their documented input layouts.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Editing registration landmarks
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Editing registration landmarks. Select Nasion, Inion, LPA or RPA in the viewer's edit landmarks panel, or click its yellow cube. MRI fiducial diamonds are editable too. Enter X/Y/Z in millimeters and Apply coordinates. Entries are constrained to the displayed scalp by default; uncheck the constraint for an exact off-surface coordinate. Snap to scalp projects the current point. Pick on scalp places it at your next click on the head; Escape cancels. Rotate first to expose the desired side. Direction buttons take a step in the local tangent plane and project back onto the scalp triangles. The step is a tangent displacement, not a geodesic distance. Reset selected restores the pipeline position. Edits are kept per dataset in browser storage when available; Export JSON downloads them with frame metadata. For reconstructed subjects, save the exported file as saves/subjects//corrections.json and rerun python ingestsubject.py to apply corrections and recompute EEG positions. Original input files stay unchanged. Template edits do not recompute Monte Carlo registration/statistics. Changed source landmark exports invalidate saved browser edits. Regenerate the MNI demo with python runpipeline.py --template for explicit MNI152NLin2009aSym metadata. Primary patient coordinates remain native subject RAS even when secondary MNI coordinates are available. See the MNI migration plan for the source audit and rollout.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Aim 1 statistics
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Aim 1 statistics. Put Brainsight session exports in saves/brainsight/ named sub-coilposesamples.txt, with samples named sub-EEGCAPPOSEREP and sub-MRIPOSEREP. bash python analysis/aim1stats.py This prints per-site statistics and writes saves/aim1/measurements.csv (one row per compared placement), saves/aim1/aim1stats.csv (one number per row), and viewer/src/data/aim1stats.json. Methods live in src/stats.py and use statsmodels.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Aim 2 electric-field modeling
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Aim 2 electric-field modeling. See the electric-field workflow for SimNIBS setup, head models, coil poses, individualized target coordinates and dry-run commands. SimNIBS uses its own interpreter; it is not installed into this venv. runpipeline.py does not run tissue segmentation or electric-field simulations.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Tests
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Tests. The viewer's scalp projection and movement tests run with Node.js: bash cd viewer node --test tests/landmarkGeometry.test.mjs cd .. Use the same venv, from the repository root: bash python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt python -m pytest tests/ Input tests use temporary files and mocked downloads. They cover fallback, cohort discovery, exclusions, duplicates, collisions and mesh orientation for both affine handednesses.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: GitHub Pages
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — GitHub Pages. bash cd viewer npm run deploy Deployment checks every processed head against viewer/public-subjects.json, builds viewer/dist/ and pushes it to gh-pages. Patient datasets must never be added to that allowlist. The six legacy entries reference SimNIBS example data (Ernie: CC BY-NC 4.0; group dataset: ODC-PDDL). The MNI demo has its own attribution. Before public deployment, remove patient dataset folders from viewer/src/data/ and regenerate the registry with python runpipeline.py --template. Moving input scans alone does not remove generated meshes. Review whether the aggregate aim1stats.json should be included too. In repository settings choose Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages → / (root). The site appears at https://.github.io/TMS-Nav/; build paths are relative.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Embedding
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Embedding. html .github.io/TMS-Nav/?embed=1" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0" loading="lazy" title="TMS-Nav viewer" ?embed=1 folds both side panels and adds a link to the full page. Frames narrower than 760 px or shorter than 520 px also fold the panels.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: Template attribution
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — Template attribution. The MNI demo uses the ICBM152 nonlinear 2009 atlas distributed through Nilearn. See McGill's atlas description and license for references and full redistribution terms. Copyright (C) 1993–2004 Louis Collins, McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, Montreal Neurological Institute, McGill University. Redistribution requires retaining the copyright notice; the linked license includes the complete warranty statement.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: EEG 10–20 scalp marking
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — EEG 10–20 scalp marking. Run python runpipeline.py --template for the demo, or ingest a subject and confirm its four anatomical anchors as described in the subject workflow, then rebuild the viewer with npm run build in viewer/. The 10–20 electrodes and 10–20 dashed arcs layer switches independently control the cyan scalp sites and tape constructions. Click a site to read its physical coordinates: MNI RAS mm on the template, native subject RAS mm on an unregistered patient scan. The pipeline measures connected plane/scalp intersections by arc length: Nz–Iz at 10/30/50/70/90% gives Fpz/Fz/Cz/Pz/Oz; LPA–Cz–RPA gives T3/C3/C4/T4 at 10/30/70/90%. The full Fpz–Oz circumference supplies Fp1/F7/T5/O1 or Fp2/F8/T6/O2 at 5/15/35/45% measured from Fpz along the respective side. Transverse midpoints on F7–Fz–F8 and T5–Pz–T6 provide initial F3/F4 and P3/P4 estimates. The final sites are the intersections of those transverse arcs with the longitudinal Fp1–C3–O1 and Fp2–C4–O2 arcs, so each marker lies on both displayed guides. SMA is halfway along Fz–Cz, at 40% of Nz–Iz, rather than a fixed centimeter offset. SMA and Fpz/Oz are included with the 19 conventional scalp electrodes; A1/A2 recording references are not inferred from LPA/RPA. T3/T4/T5/T6 correspond to modern T7/T8/P7/P8 labels.

chunks.title: TMS-Nav README: EEG 10–20 scalp marking
chunks.text: TMS-Nav README — EEG 10–20 scalp marking. The dashed guides also include Fp1–C3–O1 and Fp2–C4–O2 longitudinal scalp arcs. They share the dashed-arcs layer switch. Intersection reconciliation replaces the independent transverse midpoint rule for F3/F4/P3/P4; eegqc.transversemidpointshiftmm reports each resulting displacement. The workbook calculator retains its separate Fz–F8 midpoint recipe. markers.json stores electrodes, eegarcs and eegqc. The viewer reports the sagittal-versus-coronal Cz gap; QC also records temporal-versus-ring midpoint gaps. Plane cuts approximate snug tape paths on the reconstructed scalp, and independent constructions can disagree on an irregular head. Landmark heuristics still need review, particularly on defaced scans. Old exports without EEG fields continue to load. The cyan EEG cap is separate from the existing approximate MRI target markers and Monte Carlo results. These five targets are fixed-direction scalp placeholders, not anatomically selected Brainsight targets; see the target-definition audit. Browser point edits hide the cap until saved corrections are applied by subject ingestion. Unconfirmed subject anchors withhold the cap rather than assign precise positions. Subject views do not display Monte Carlo dots or template target placeholders. Marking reference: Seeck et al., IFCN standardized electrode array (2017).

chunks.title: LapseCam README: LapseCam
chunks.text: LapseCam README — LapseCam. Windows app I built to turn study sessions into time-lapses. Record your screen, webcam, or both, hit stop, and you get a sped-up video. No editing step after. Website: lapsecam.alirad.dev

chunks.title: LapseCam README: Download
chunks.text: LapseCam README — Download. Get the installer or portable exe from the releases page. Works on Windows 10/11. The exe isn't code signed (those certs are expensive), so SmartScreen will complain the first time. Click "More info" then "Run anyway", or build from source below. To confirm your download is intact, compare its SHA-256 against SHA256SUMS.txt on the release: Get-FileHash .\LapseCam-1.2.0-setup.exe

chunks.title: LapseCam README: How it works
chunks.text: LapseCam README — How it works. Instead of recording full video and speeding it up later, LapseCam grabs one photo every few seconds and writes it to disk. When you stop, ffmpeg stitches the frames into a video at whatever speed you picked. Only one frame sits in memory at a time, so long sessions stay lightweight. Features: - Screen only, webcam only, or screen with a draggable webcam overlay - Draggable blur regions to hide sensitive on-screen content - Speed presets from 30x to 600x, or custom interval + fps - Elapsed time stamped into the video, optional floating timer (excluded from capture) - Pause/resume without splitting the session - Auto-stop after a set number of hours - Exports MP4, WebM, MOV, or GIF - Check for updates on launch - Everything stays local

chunks.title: LapseCam README: Build
chunks.text: LapseCam README — Build. npm run dist Output lands in dist/ (installer, portable exe, and SHA256SUMS.txt). Upload all three to the GitHub release so the checksums on the site and README stay verifiable. Run npm run icon to regenerate build/icon.ico. It's a tiny script that draws the icon pixel by pixel (matching site/favicon.svg) so I didn't have to mess with an image editor.

chunks.title: LapseCam README: Code signing
chunks.text: LapseCam README — Code signing. The download works fine, but SmartScreen warns because the exe is unsigned. Signing is the only thing that removes the warning. Options, cheapest first: - SignPath Foundation — free code signing for eligible open-source projects. - Certum Open Source Code Signing — around $70/year. - Azure Trusted Signing — around $10/month if you qualify. Once you have a certificate, add it to build.win in package.json. For a local .pfx (Certum etc.): json "win": { "signtoolOptions": { "certificateFile": "path/to/cert.pfx", "certificatePassword": "..." } } For Azure Trusted Signing, set AZURE env vars and add an azureSignOptions block per the electron-builder docs. Keep the certificate and password out of git.

chunks.title: LapseCam README: Layout
chunks.text: LapseCam README — Layout. src/main/ electron main process, IPC, ffmpeg src/renderer/ UI and capture loop scripts/ gen-icon.js, set-exe-icon.js, gen-checksums.js (post-build) site/ landing page

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: Dynamic Wallpapers
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — Dynamic Wallpapers. Lock screen wallpapers that update themselves every day. Pick something to track (the current year, your life in weeks, a countdown to a goal, or progress through any date range), point your phone at a URL, and the image quietly refreshes every morning. No app to install, no account, no database. Live site: https://dynamicwallpapers.alirad.dev

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: The idea
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — The idea. Most people glance at their lock screen dozens of times a day. I wanted that glance to carry a small bit of meaning, like a reminder that the year is 60% gone or that a deadline is 12 days away, without piling on another notification or app. It all runs on one simple trick. An image URL renders a fresh PNG every time it is requested, so you set up a daily automation once (Shortcuts on iPhone, MacroDroid on Android) and then forget about it. The wallpaper keeps itself current.

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: What it does
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — What it does. - Year: a grid of every day in the year, with the days so far filled in and today highlighted - Life: one square for every week you have lived, counted from your date of birth - Goal: a countdown ring to a date that matters, showing the days left - Progress: a percent bar through any start and end date Each style comes with light and dark themes, five accent colors, and resolution presets for common iPhone, iPad, and Android screens so nothing gets cropped.

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: How it works
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — How it works. Every endpoint (/api/year, /api/life, /api/goal, /api/progress) takes a handful of query params and returns a PNG: /api/goal?goal=Ship+the+app&goaldate=2026-12-31&theme=dark The layout is drawn as an SVG on the server and rasterized to a PNG with sharp. The browser preview builds the exact same SVG on the client, so what you see while setting things up is what actually lands on your phone. The hard part was text. When you rasterize SVG text on a server, the output depends on whatever fonts happen to be installed, which changes from one machine to the next. To get around that, I convert every label into vector path outlines from the real font file before rasterizing. The text then comes out pixel for pixel identical everywhere, with no font dependency at runtime.

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: Tech stack
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — Tech stack. - Next.js (App Router) and TypeScript - Tailwind CSS for the UI - Framer Motion for the setup wizard - sharp for SVG to PNG rasterizing - opentype.js for converting text into font outlines - Hosted on Netlify

chunks.title: Dynamic Wallpapers README: What I learned
chunks.text: Dynamic Wallpapers README — What I learned. - Rendering text reliably on a server is far trickier than it sounds. Outlining glyphs myself forced me to actually understand font units, glyph advances, and how a typeface turns into pixels. - One source of truth is worth the effort. The same SVG builder feeds both the live preview and the final image, so the two can never fall out of sync. - Fewer moving parts is a feature. Dropping accounts and a database kept the app cheap to run and pushed the real logic into small, pure functions that are easy to test. - The last mile of UX is all details. Figuring out how to stop iOS from cropping the image took plenty of trial and error, and writing that up clearly saves every user the same frustration.

chunks.title: MarketScope README: Stock Performance Dashboard
chunks.text: MarketScope README — Stock Performance Dashboard. A web app to track and compare stock performance using Python and Streamlit.

chunks.title: MarketScope README: What it does
chunks.text: MarketScope README — What it does. - Enter multiple stock tickers (like AAPL, MSFT, TSLA) - Select a date range (30 days, 90 days, 6 months, or 1 year) - View performance metrics and charts comparing the stocks

chunks.title: MarketScope README: Technologies
chunks.text: MarketScope README — Technologies. - yfinance - Gets stock data from Yahoo Finance - pandas - Processes the data - matplotlib - Creates charts - Streamlit - Web interface

chunks.title: MarketScope README: How to run
chunks.text: MarketScope README — How to run. bash streamlit run app.py Or if that doesn't work: bash python -m streamlit run app.py The app should open in your browser at http://localhost:8501

chunks.title: MarketScope README: Features
chunks.text: MarketScope README — Features. - Compare multiple stocks at once - See latest prices, daily changes, and total percent change - View price trends over time - See which stock performed best (highlighted in green) - Sortable metrics table

chunks.title: MarketScope README: Project files
chunks.text: MarketScope README — Project files. - app.py - Main Streamlit app - stockdata.py - Functions to fetch data and calculate metrics - stockcharts.py - Functions to create charts - requirements.txt - Required packages to run the program

chunks.title: MarketScope README: Usage
chunks.text: MarketScope README — Usage. 1. Enter ticker symbols separated by commas (e.g., "AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL") 2. Choose a date range 3. Click "Analyze Stocks" 4. View the results!
